planting.note: Plant container stock in fall or spring in well-drained, acidic to neutral soil.

directions: Dapper is an English holly grown for its creamy white-variegated foliage over a forest-green base, giving a brighter, more contrasting look than plain-leaved hollies. Site it with some shelter from intense winter sun and drying wind to keep the variegation from scorching, and shear lightly to maintain a dense pyramidal outline. Remove any reverted all-green shoots promptly, as they grow faster than the variegated wood and will overtake it.

planting.note: Plant container stock in fall or spring; pair with a male English holly nearby for berry production on this female selection.

directions: Zelta's Elite is a female English holly with spiny, dark green leaves edged in soft yellowish margins, giving a more subdued variegation than brighter gold-edged cultivars. Grow in well-drained, acidic to neutral soil with some protection from scorching winter sun. Site a male English holly or Highclere hybrid nearby to pollinate the flowers and produce the classic red winter berries. Prune lightly after the berry display fades to keep the dense, pyramidal habit in check.

planting.note: Plant container stock in fall or spring in well-drained soil; this vigorous female Highclere hybrid tolerates coastal exposure better than true English holly.

directions: One of the oldest and most widely planted Ilex x altaclerensis cultivars, Wilsonii bears exceptionally large, glossy, broadly spined dark green leaves on a vigorous, dense evergreen shrub or small tree, raised at the historic Handsworth nursery within the broader Highclere hybrid group's English-holly-x-Ilex-perado breeding tradition and awarded an FCC in 1899. As a female clone it produces generous crops of red berries when a male holly is planted nearby for pollination. It tolerates urban pollution, salt spray, and partial shade better than most English holly cultivars, making it a workhorse hedging and screening plant in milder climates. Prune after fruiting to control size on this fast-growing selection.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant container stock in fall or spring; valued as one of the hardiest and most pollution-tolerant Highclere hybrid hollies for hedging, raised by Thomas Hodgins in Ireland before 1836.

directions: Hodginsii is a male Ilex x altaclerensis selection prized for its exceptional cold hardiness and wind tolerance, qualities unusual among the Highclere hybrid hollies, which let it serve as a dependable large hedge or windbreak in exposed sites. Its broad, dark green, moderately spiny leaves and purplish young stems are larger than true English holly and give the plant a bold, coarse texture, capable of withstanding heavily polluted atmospheres. Being a male clone it never fruits, but its pollen helps set berries on nearby female hollies. Grow in well-drained soil and shear in late winter to maintain a dense hedge form.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall; this narrow, upright female blue holly suits tight vertical spaces where standard meserveae cultivars would outgrow the site, and requires a male pollenizer such as Castle Wall nearby.

directions: Sold as Castle Spire, 'Hachfee' is a female blue holly bred for a narrow, dense, upright habit that fits foundation plantings and tight side-yards too small for a standard Meserve holly. Its spiny, blue-green leaves and bright red berries follow the familiar blue holly look in a fraction of the footprint. Plant a male blue holly, such as Castle Wall or Blue Prince, within range for pollination and reliable fruiting. Grow in well-drained, slightly acidic soil with some wind protection in colder zones.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall; this narrow, upright male blue holly is bred and sold explicitly as the pollinating companion to Castle Spire.

directions: Marketed as Castle Wall, 'Heckenstar' is a male blue holly selected to match the narrow, dense, upright habit of Castle Spire, making the pair a compact screening combination for sites too small for traditional Blue Prince or Blue Princess hollies. Its glossy, spiny blue-green foliage never bears berries, but its pollen is what sets fruit on female blue hollies planted nearby. Grow in well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and give it some winter wind protection at the colder end of its range.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall; patented (USPP7652) cross of Ilex aquifolium 'Fructu Luteo' x Ilex rugosa, a female sport bearing lemon-yellow berries.

directions: Golden Girl is a female Meserve blue holly selection grown for its profuse lemon-yellow berries, a departure from the red fruit typical of the Blue Prince and Blue Princess lineage, set against the same glossy, spiny, blue-green foliage. Plant a male blue holly within pollinating range to ensure a heavy berry crop for winter display. Grow in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade, with wind protection in the coldest parts of its range, and prune lightly after the fruit display fades.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall; patented (PP20049) seedling of 'Sky Pencil' with a narrow pyramidal rather than columnar habit that needs no shearing to hold shape.

directions: Sky Pointer is a Japanese holly seedling of 'Sky Pencil' selected for a naturally narrow, pyramidal silhouette that holds its shape without the regular shearing that boxwood-style plantings usually demand. Its small, boxwood-like evergreen leaves lack the spines of English or American holly, making it comfortable to plant along walkways. Grow in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, and water during establishment and dry summer stretches, since Japanese holly resents prolonged drought more than many other hollies.
sources: Spring Meadow Nursery / Proven Winners ColorChoice

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall; one of the few variegated Japanese holly cultivars, useful for brightening shade borders without holly spines.

directions: Snowflake is a female Japanese holly selected for gray-green leaves edged in creamy white, an unusual variegated option in a species normally grown for its plain, glossy, boxwood-like foliage. Its small flowers can set inconspicuous black fruit if a male Japanese holly pollinates nearby, though the foliage color is the main draw. Grow in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to protect the lighter-colored margins from scorching, and keep it consistently watered, since Japanese holly is less drought-tolerant than American hollies.
sources: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox — Ilex crenata

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall; its densely branched upright habit makes a tidy low hedge or foundation planting with minimal pruning.

directions: Twiggy is a female Japanese holly selected for an upright, densely branched growth habit that forms a tidy, uniform hedge or low screen with little shaping. Its small, glossy, spineless leaves resemble boxwood and give winter structure without the sharp edges of English or American holly. Grow in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, and water during dry spells, since this species is shallow-rooted and more drought-sensitive than it appears.
sources: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox — Ilex crenata

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall; a rounded dwarf form useful as a boxwood substitute with the bonus of yellow fruit on female plants.

directions: Geisha is a female Japanese holly with a naturally rounded, dwarf habit that closely mimics boxwood, right down to the small, spineless, glossy leaves, but it carries the bonus of yellow fruit where boxwood offers none. It works well as a low hedge, edging plant, or clipped globe in formal borders. Grow in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, and water consistently during establishment, since Japanese holly's shallow roots make it less drought-tolerant than many other broadleaf evergreens.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; a Monrovia-patented seedling selection of 'Interhydia' (Pink Diamond) bred for an earlier, deeper blush.

directions: Bred by Monrovia as a seedling of 'Interhydia' (Pink Diamond) and patented as 'Ruby', Angel's Blush produces large conical panicles that open white and blush to a rosy pink earlier and more intensely than its Pink Diamond parent. Grow in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; like other panicle hydrangeas it is unaffected by soil pH, unlike bigleaf hydrangeas grown for blue or pink mophead color. It flowers on new wood, so prune hard in late winter to control size without losing the current season's blooms, and deadhead spent panicles once they fade.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil; this dwarf, mounding selection fits small gardens and containers where full-size Grandiflora would overwhelm the space. Note: a distinct, unrelated cultivar of the same name also exists in Hydrangea quercifolia (oakleaf hydrangea).

directions: Pee Wee is a naturally dwarf sport of the old 'Grandiflora' (Pee Gee) panicle hydrangea, keeping the same rounded white flower cones but on a low, dense, mounded shrub roughly a third the size of its parent. Flowers open white, age to soft green, and finish with a pink blush in fall, held on sturdy stems that need little staking. Grow in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; it tolerates heat and is unaffected by soil pH, unlike bigleaf hydrangeas. Prune in late winter if needed, since it blooms on new wood and tolerates hard cutback without losing the season's flowers.
